intents.name: Data Locality and Reuse Optimization
intents.description: Restructure iteration space and data layout to maximize temporal and spatial reuse within the CPU cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3).
intents.rationale: Dense loop nests have high arithmetic intensity but only realize it when working sets fit in cache. Without locality optimizations, memory bandwidth becomes the bottleneck despite abundant compute reuse. This is the foundational optimization category for all high-performance CPU kernels.

transformations.name: Tiling
transformations.description: Partition the iteration space into multi-dimensional blocks so that the data accessed within each block fits in a target cache level.
transformations.rationale: Tiling is the most impactful single transformation for loop nests on CPU. It converts O(N) cache misses into O(N/B) by ensuring temporal reuse within cache-resident blocks. Multi-level tiling maps naturally to the L1/L2/L3 hierarchy.
transformations.action_template: Tiling(tile_sizes) — tile_sizes is a vector with one entry per loop dimension; 0 means do not tile that dimension. OR Tiling(loop_band, tile_sizes) — tile_sizes applied to a specific loop band.

transformations.name: Packing
transformations.description: Copy data accessed within a tile into a contiguous buffer with a layout optimized for sequential access, eliminating stride and TLB penalties.
transformations.rationale: After tiling, sub-arrays within a tile may still suffer from non-unit-stride access and cache conflict misses. Packing rearranges data into contiguous micro-panels, which is the standard technique in optimized BLAS libraries for achieving near-peak throughput.
transformations.action_template: Packing(packed_sizes) — packed_sizes is a vector with one entry per iterator dimension; 0 means do not pack along that dimension. OR Packing(loop_band, packed_sizes).

intents.name: SIMD and Instruction-Level Performance
intents.description: Exploit vector instruction sets (AVX2+FMA) and instruction-level parallelism to maximize single-core computational throughput.
intents.rationale: The target CPU can issue 2 FMA operations per cycle on 256-bit vectors (4 FP64 lanes). Without vectorization, peak throughput drops by 4x for FP64. Without unrolling, pipeline bubbles and loop overhead prevent sustained FMA utilization.

transformations.name: Vectorization
transformations.description: Map one or more innermost loop dimensions to SIMD vector lanes, enabling AVX2 vector load/store/FMA instructions.
transformations.rationale: Vectorization is essential to utilize the 256-bit FMA units. For FP64, each vector instruction processes 4 elements simultaneously. The transformation ensures the target dimension has contiguous memory access and sufficient trip count for efficient vector execution.
transformations.action_template: Vectorization(vector_sizes) — vector_sizes is a vector with one entry per loop dimension specifying the vector width for that dimension; all entries must be positive and their product must not exceed 1024.

transformations.name: Loop Unrolling
transformations.description: Replicate the loop body across multiple consecutive iterations of a chosen dimension, exposing independent operations and enabling register-level data reuse.
transformations.rationale: Unrolling amortizes loop control overhead, exposes independent FMA operations to the out-of-order engine, and creates register tiles that maximize data reuse across unrolled iterations. It is the primary mechanism for filling FMA pipelines and reducing loop-carried dependency stalls.
transformations.action_template: LoopUnrolling(dimension, unroll_factor) — dimension is the 0-indexed loop to unroll; unroll_factor is the number of loop body copies.

intents.name: Loop Structure and Thread-Level Parallelism
intents.description: Reorder loop dimensions and distribute iteration space across threads to improve memory access patterns and exploit multi-core parallelism.
intents.rationale: Loop ordering determines memory access stride patterns (affecting vectorization legality and cache line utilization) and which loops are candidates for parallel distribution. With 28 cores available, thread-level parallelism provides significant speedup for large problem sizes, but requires careful loop structuring to avoid false sharing and NUMA penalties.

transformations.name: Loop Interchange
transformations.description: Permute the ordering of loops in a loop nest to improve memory access patterns, enable vectorization of the innermost loop, or place parallel loops outermost.
transformations.rationale: In a multi-dimensional loop nest, the loop order directly controls whether innermost accesses are stride-1 (cache-friendly, vectorizable) or strided. Interchange is often a prerequisite for effective vectorization and parallelization, and can dramatically reduce cache misses by aligning iteration order with data layout.
transformations.action_template: LoopInterchange(permutation) — permutation is a list of 0-based loop indices specifying the new loop order; must be a non-identity permutation. OR LoopInterchange(loop_band, permutation).

transformations.name: Parallelization
transformations.description: Distribute iterations of one or more outer parallel loops across multiple threads for concurrent execution on the multi-core CPU.
transformations.rationale: The target machine has 28 physical cores across 2 NUMA nodes. For large loop nests, parallelizing outer dimensions provides near-linear speedup. The transformation must target loops with no loop-carried dependencies (parallel loops) and use appropriate granularity to balance load and minimize synchronization overhead.
transformations.action_template: Parallelization(num_threads) — num_threads is the number of threads to distribute work across.
